title: Catch Me If You Can Was Probably a Lie
sentences: Frank Abagnale became famous for saying he faked being a pilot, a doctor and a lawyer as a teenager.
His story became a bestselling book and a Hollywood film.
But in 2020, researcher Alan Logan dug through old records and found serious problems.
Records placed Abagnale in prison in the years he claimed he was flying around the world.
Former colleagues and documents contradicted many of his most famous adventures.
Abagnale did commit real fraud, but much of the legend appears to have been invented.
The greatest con may have been the story itself.
How much of a famous story do you just believe?

title: 3 Men Escaped Alcatraz Using Fake Heads Made of Soap
sentences: In June 1962, guards at Alcatraz found three prisoners asleep in their beds.
Except they were not prisoners at all, they were heads made from soap, paper and real hair.
Frank Morris and brothers John and Clarence Anglin had dug through their cell walls with sharpened spoons.
They climbed onto the roof and launched a raft made from more than fifty raincoats.
Then they disappeared into the cold waters of San Francisco Bay.
The FBI concluded they most likely drowned, but no bodies were ever found.
The case is still officially open with the US Marshals today.
Do you think they made it?

title: Fake Doctor Performed Surgery on a Warship and Got Away With It
sentences: In 1951, a Canadian navy destroyer had a new doctor on board named Joseph Cyr.
During the Korean War, he operated on wounded soldiers and saved lives.
But he was not a doctor, he was an impostor named Ferdinand Waldo Demara.
He had borrowed the real doctor's identity and learned what he could from medical books.
His fame finally exposed him, when newspapers reported the doctor's heroics.
The real Joseph Cyr saw the story and realised someone was using his name.
Demara was sent home, and spent his life switching identities again and again.
Could you fake a job you never trained for?

title: He Promised 50% Profit in 45 Days and Fooled Thousands
sentences: In 1920, Charles Ponzi promised investors in Boston a 50 percent return in just 45 days.
He claimed the money came from trading international postal coupons.
In reality, he paid early investors with money from new investors.
Thousands of people lined up, and he was taking in huge sums every day.
A newspaper investigation showed his business could never make that money.
Within months it collapsed, and Ponzi went to prison for fraud.
His name is still used for every scheme that works the same way.
Have you ever seen an offer that sounded too good?

title: Innocent Man Jailed Twice Because He Had a Lookalike
sentences: In 1896, London police arrested Adolf Beck after a woman said he had tricked her.
Several women identified him as a con man who stole their jewellery.
Beck said he was innocent, but he was convicted and sent to prison.
After his release, he was arrested and convicted again for the same kind of crime.
Then, while Beck was in custody, the real con man kept committing the crimes.
The real culprit, a man who looked like Beck, was caught, and Beck was pardoned.
The scandal helped lead to England's Court of Criminal Appeal in 1907.
Should one witness be enough to convict someone?

title: She Raised $700M With a Blood Test That Didn't Work
sentences: Elizabeth Holmes said her company, Theranos, could run hundreds of tests from a drop of blood.
Investors poured in hundreds of millions of dollars, and the company was valued at 9 billion.
But the machines did not work the way she claimed.
Many tests were secretly run on ordinary lab machines from other companies.
A Wall Street Journal reporter exposed the problems in 2015.
In 2022, Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors and later sentenced to over eleven years.
A whistleblower and a reporter brought down a billion-dollar lie.
Would you have invested?

title: 76 Prisoners Escaped the Nazis Through a Tunnel Called Harry
sentences: In 1944, Allied airmen in a German prison camp called Stalag Luft Three dug three secret tunnels.
They named them Tom, Dick and Harry, so the guards would never hear the word tunnel.
Sand from digging was hidden in bags inside their trousers and shaken out in the gardens.
Bed boards held up the walls, and a hand-pumped air system kept the diggers breathing.
On the night of March 24th, 76 men crawled through Harry and out beyond the fence.
Almost all were caught, and only three made it all the way to freedom.
The story became the famous film The Great Escape.
Would you have crawled into that tunnel?

title: 109 Officers Escaped Prison Through a Tunnel Dug With Spoons
sentences: In 1864, Union officers were held in Libby Prison, a crowded warehouse in Richmond, Virginia.
A group of them found a way into a rat-filled cellar the guards rarely checked.
For weeks, they dug a tunnel using knives, spoons and a wooden spittoon to drag out dirt.
On February 9th, 109 officers crawled through it and walked out into the city.
Guards did not notice until the morning roll call came up short.
Fifty-nine of them reached Union lines, one of the biggest prison breaks of the Civil War.
Would you trust a tunnel dug with spoons?

title: Robbers Came for $3M Cash and Found $35M in Gold
sentences: In November 1983, six robbers broke into the Brink's-Mat warehouse near Heathrow Airport in London.
They had inside help from a security guard, and expected to find about three million pounds in cash.
Instead, they found nearly 7,000 gold bars worth around 26 million pounds.
They loaded it all into a van and drove away.
Much of the gold was melted down and quietly sold back into the market.
Some robbers were caught, but most of the gold has never been found.
People say anyone wearing gold bought in Britain after 1983 might be wearing some of it.
Would you check your jewellery?

title: He Mailed Himself to Freedom in a Wooden Box
sentences: In 1849, Henry Brown was enslaved in Richmond, Virginia, and his family had been sold away.
He decided to escape in the most dangerous way possible: by shipping himself in a box.
The crate was about three feet long, with a few holes for air and a little water.
For about 27 hours, it travelled by wagon, train and steamboat, sometimes upside down.
It arrived at an anti-slavery office in Philadelphia, and when they opened it, he climbed out.
He became known as Henry Box Brown, and spoke across America and Britain about his escape.
Could you survive 27 hours in a box?
